# Pronouncing Omononushi: a guide for the curious

Saying **Omononushi** aloud requires more than reading Latin letters ​on a screen. The conventional spelling is only the entry point into a reconstructed sound and a much older tradition. This post unpacks that sound, the Japanese characters evidence, the kindred forms, ‌and the mythological record, then shows how the temple preserves the whole argument without pretending that a diacritic was ever lost.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Omononushi
- **ASCII form:** omononushi
- **Meaning:** "Great ‌thing lord"
- **Domain of influence:** Mountains, Deity of Miwa
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 大物忌神 (Japanese characters)

## Overview

**Omononushi** (*omononushi*) — Mountains, Deity of Miwa · Great thing lord — ​belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Mountains, Deity of Miwa". The name means "Great thing lord".

**Ōmononushi** is the mysterious kami of Mount Miwa, one of ​the oldest and most enigmatic deities in Japan. He is associated with snakes, oracles, and the transfer of the land to Amaterasu's descendants. Unlike most kami, he had no image and was ​worshipped in the form of the mountain itself.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Omononushi** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/omononushi/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from ​the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *omononushi* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## ​The Name

The name is attested in Japanese characters as **大物忌神**. Etymologically it means "Great thing lord".

The canonical spelling **Omononushi** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *omononushi* contains ‌the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. ## The Original Script

The name is written in Japanese characters as **大物忌神**. That attested script remains the primary evidence for the conventional romanization **Omononushi**. The canonical Latin ​spelling does not pretend to recover marks it never contained: it fixes one reviewed reference form while leaving the original script visible for comparison.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is ‌**/o.mo.no.nɯ.ɕi/** — Modern Standard Japanese (Hepburn).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **O-** — Open-mid back [o]
- **-mo-** — Bilabial [m] plus open-mid [o]; from 物 'thing'
- **-no-** — Alveolar nasal [n] plus open-mid [o]
- ​**-nushi** — Alveolar nasal [n], close back [ɯ], voiceless alveolo-palatal [ɕ], close front [i]; from 主 'lord/master'

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'OH-moh-noh-noo-shee' — even syllables, with soft final ‌vowels.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Japanese** — 大物忌神 (Ōmononushi-no-kami), 'Great Thing Lord'
- **Other names** — Miwa-no-kami; identified with Ōkuninushi (Ōnamuji) in some traditions
- **Cult center** — Ōmiwa Shrine at ​Mount Miwa, Nara

Omononushi keeps its restoration plain: plain Hepburn. He is an ancient mountain deity associated with Miwa and the land-transfer myth.

## Mythology

Ōmononushi's mythology is preserved in strange, archaic tales ​of snakes, possession, and oracles — the Kojiki's strangest marriage, the constitution of Japan's sovereignty, and a shrine with no god-house, because the mountain is the god.

### The Serpent Husband of Ikutamayori ​(Kojiki)

A maiden named Ikutamayori was visited each night by a beautiful man who came unseen. When she bore his child, her parents demanded to know the father. She had him leave ​a needle threaded with red silk in the hem of his garment; in the morning she followed the thread, and it led to the foot of Mount Miwa and vanished into a ​cave — where the visitor declared himself: he was *Ōmononushi*, the great lord of the mountain, and he appeared in serpent form. The child of this union was Kotoshironushi, the god who ‌would one day counsel the peaceful surrender of the land to the heavenly grandson (Kojiki; cf. Nihon Shoki, Aston's translation).

The tale binds three things into one knot — mountain, snake, and ​the Miwa priestly line, whose descent from the kami's human bride it exists to explain.

### The Oracle of the Land (Kojiki · Nihon Shoki)

When the heavenly emissary Takemikazuchi descended to demand ‌the land from the earthly god Ōnamuji (Ōkuninushi), Ōnamuji consulted his children. Kotoshironushi, away at Cape Miwa, answered that resistance to the heavenly grandson was hopeless — and then all eyes turned ​to the mountain. Ōmononushi was consulted, and his oracle settled the matter: 'Let the land be given over in peace,' he declared; the land was yielded, and he withdrew into a hidden ‌realm, promising that his favor would attend his proper worship. The Nihon Shoki tells the same event differently, folding the mountain god into Ōnamuji himself: Ōnamuji, it says, is also called Ōmononushi ​(Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, tr. Aston, I).

Here the god is pure voice: sovereignty changes hands in Japan not by conquest but by consultation — and the mountain kami's consent is the constitution.

### ‌The Bride of Miwa (Kojiki)

Ōmononushi took as wife Seyadatarahime, daughter of his own son Kotoshironushi by Ikutamayori — and their child was the princess Himetataraisuzuhime. She became the consort of Emperor ​Sujin and bore the future Emperor Suinin: the serpent-god of Mount Miwa thus entered the imperial genealogy itself, the god's line becoming grandmother to the next sovereign. The Kojiki's genealogy is compressed and ‌the texts do not spell every step out plainly, but the dynastic point stands: the mountain married into the house that received the mountain's realm.

The marriage also sealed an alliance between ​the Miwa priestly house and the court — the god who gave the land away kept his blood beside the throne. The Kojiki records the whole sequence without wonder, as plain genealogy: ​which is how one knows the text was compiled on the winning side.

### The Plague and the Possessed Princess (Kojiki · Nihon Shoki)

In Emperor Sujin's reign plague and disaster struck the ‌land, and divination named the cause: the great kami of Mount Miwa, never yet given a shrine, was angry. The god made his will known by possessing a princess of his own ‌line and speaking through her: worship me, he demanded, and I will cause the land to flourish. Sujin founded the rites; the pestilence lifted. The Nihon Shoki's parallel account likewise has the ‌god speak through a human mouth, claim credit for guiding the cession of the land, and demand his due — the god of Miwa and the god of the land-transfer asserted as ​one and the same (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, Aston I).

Myth here explains a liturgy: Ōmiwa's worship began, the texts insist, when the neglected mountain finally raised its voice.

### Worship without Image (Cult)

​Ōmiwa Shrine, at the foot of the mountain in Nara prefecture, is one of Japan's oldest shrines and one of the strangest: it has no *honden*, no inner sanctuary housing a divine ‌image, because the god is not symbolized by anything — the god *is* Mount Miwa. Worshippers pray toward the peak across a unique three-pillared torii, the Miwa-torii; before the worship hall stand ​sacred sake casks, for Ōmononushi is patron of the brewers of Miwa, and his serpent form — a great snake said to coil in the mountain's caves — was traditionally offered sake. ​First listed among the great shrines in the Engishiki (927 CE), the site preserves a stratum of Japanese religion older than images: the mountain itself as *shintai*, the deity's body.

The absent ‌statue is the theology: what has no face cannot be owned, and what cannot be owned cannot be conquered.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Omononushi concentrates in a small set ​of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Mount Miwa** — The mountain itself, worshipped as the kami's body — his true shintai
- **Snake** — The form in which Ōmononushi ​appears in the Ikutamayori legend — the sacred without a face
- **Sake** — Offered to the serpent-kami; Ōmononushi is patron of the brewers of Miwa, honored with sugitama cedar balls
- **The Miwa-torii** ‌— The unique three-pillared torii through which worshippers face the peak directly — architecture that frames a god who is geology

## Archaeology & Evidence

The Engishiki shrine register (927 CE) already lists ​Ōmiwa among the great sanctuaries, and the site's archaeology is deep: excavations around Miwa have yielded ritual deposits and prestige objects — bronze mirrors, swords, and beads — from the Yayoi-to-Kofun transition, ‌indicating a sanctuary of unusual antiquity at the mountain's foot, and the great keyhole tomb Hashihaka nearby marks the district as an early center of power. No honden has ever stood at ​Ōmiwa; worship runs toward the peak through the unique Miwa-torii, whose third central pillar frames the mountain as the true sanctuary. The 'artifact' of this god is thus geological and botanical at ​once — bedrock, cedar, and the spring-water sake that the shrine has brewed since the rite began.

## Realm & Domain

**Ōmononushi** is the mysterious kami of Mount Miwa, one of the oldest ​and most enigmatic deities in Japan. He is associated with snakes, oracles, and the transfer of the land to Amaterasu's descendants. Unlike most kami, he had no image and was worshipped in ​the form of the mountain itself.

### Mountain God

He is identified with Mount Miwa itself; Ōmiwa Shrine has no inner sanctuary because the peak is the kami's body.

### Snake Deity

He comes ‌to Ikutamayori as a serpent in the Kojiki, and snake offerings of sake attend his Miwa cult.

### Oracle Kami

His consent to the land-transfer was given by oracle — sovereignty in Japan ‌changes hands by consultation, not conquest.

### Land Transfer

He is the voice that yields the land to the heavenly descendants, binding the Miwa line to the imperial house.

## Across Cultures

Ōmononushi never ​left Shinto, but he was folded into it from two directions. The Nihon Shoki already identifies him with Ōkuninushi — the local Miwa kami gathered into the imperial land-myth — and medieval ‌*honji suijaku* doctrine went further: Mount Miwa's deity, as Miwa Daimyōjin, was given the Buddhist original ground of Śākyamuni Buddha, and Miwa mandalas picture the mountain with Buddhist cosmography laid over it. ​Under the mountain, ascetics of the Shugendō tradition practiced until the modern period, treating the peak itself as the object of cult. The serpent, the sake, and the oracle — archaic, local, ​and oracular — are precisely the features a centralizing mythology needed to absorb rather than erase: Ōmononushi survives because he was useful, first to the court that took his oracle, then to ‌the Buddhism that crowned him, then to the brewers who still hang cedar balls for him.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[anahita|Anāhitā]], [[audhumla|Auðhumla]], [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[bastet|Bꜣstt]], [[cernunnos|Cernunnos]], and [[coatlicue|Cōātlīcue]], each ‌linked through earth / mother / fertility.

## Cultural Legacy

Ōmiwa Shrine still stands where the myth says it must: at the foot of Mount Miwa, without a main hall, prayer aimed at ‌the peak. The surrounding district remains sacred geography — Isonokami, one of Japan's oldest shrines, close by, and the great early kofun of Hashihaka on the horizon. Miwa sake is still brewed under ‌the god's patronage, and brewers across Japan hang *sugitama* cedar balls in his honor. The mountain appears in Nara-period poetry, and the Miwa-torii's third pillar is studied wherever shrine architecture is taught. ​For modern Shinto, Ōmononushi is the standing proof that the kami need not be anthropomorphic: his 'image' is a modest ridge of green rock and cedar, and on clear mornings the faithful ‌still bow toward it before entering the shrine.

## The Scholarly Record

The account of Omononushi given in this edition rests on the witnesses and reference works listed below. Lexica and etymological dictionaries ​secure the form and meaning of the name; the literary and religious texts supply the narrative evidence.

-  Kojiki — the Ikutamayori serpent legend, the land-transfer oracle, the marriage to Seyadatarahime, the Sujin ​plague cycle.
-  Nihon Shoki — parallel land-transfer and Sujin accounts; Ōnamuji 'also called Ōmononushi'.
-  Engishiki Jinmyōchō (927) — Ōmiwa among the registered great shrines.
-  Philippi, The Kojiki (1968).
-  Aston, Nihongi: Chronicles of ​Japan (1896).

## A Meditation

Ōmononushi is the god who refuses to be a person. Every other great kami of Japan acquired a face, a genealogy, a palace in the poems; Ōmononushi acquired ‌a mountain, and the mountain — unportable, unburnable, unshippable — has guarded his integrity ever since. He enters myth only as a voice or a snake: the two forms in which the ​sacred appears without becoming an idol. His oracle teaches a politics as well: the land changed hands because he consented, and consent, not conquest, is what his cult claims as the first ​principle of sovereignty. Even his marriage reads like an essay in legitimacy, wedding the mountain's line to the dynasty that received the mountain's realm. And because there is no statue, every visit ​to Ōmiwa is a small reenactment of the discovery of the sacred — you look up from the torii, past the sake casks, at green rock and cedar, and understand that you ‌have been inside the shrine since the road.
